rationale: The final sentence is ill-formed: the positive-degree part S_+=\bigoplus_{n>0}S_n is generally not an S_0-algebra (it has no unit). Standard graded should say that S itself is generated as an S_0-algebra by finitely many degree-one elements.
Step 1.2 uses the tensor/direct-sum identification \(X\otimes_R(N\oplus N')\cong(X\otimes_RN)\oplus(X\otimes_RN')\), but cites only [L1]; [L1] does not license this move. It should cite [L2].

Without a lower bound on the nonzero M_n, \sum_{n\in\mathbb Z}H_M(n)t^n is not a formal Laurent series in the standard sense (which has finitely many negative powers). The definition needs a bounded-below hypothesis or a different ambient object for bilateral series.

The transition maps \(\varphi_n\) are never required to be \(R\)-linear. With arbitrary arrows the compatible tuples need not form a submodule, so calling the displayed set an inverse-limit submodule is unjustified.

Step 3.1 applies step 2.1 to \(S^{-1}N\) without establishing its required hypothesis that \(S^{-1}N\) is flat over \(R\). [L3] gives only an isomorphism; one must also prove that \(S^{-1}R\otimes_RN\) is \(R\)-flat.

Step 1.4 invokes the theorem for the r-1-variable algebra S' as an “algebra hypothesis,” but no induction hypothesis is stated or established. Steps 1.1–1.3 alone do not license rationality/polynomial growth for K and C, so the proof has an essential gap.

Step 1.3 asserts that localization commutes with tensor products and identifies the localized kernel with \(K_{\mathfrak m}\), but cites only [L2]. The ideal-injection criterion does not license either localization claim; the required tensor/localization exactness fact is uncited.
[L2] misstates its citation: the cited definition only defines \(\ker f=\{m:f(m)=0\}\); it does not assert that the kernel is a submodule. Thus [L2] is stronger than its cited item.

The final quotient is generally undefined: t is not in \mathcal R(I), and t\mathcal R(M_\bullet) need not lie in \mathcal R(M_\bullet). For M_n=I^nM its degree n+1 terms are I^nMt^{n+1}, not generally contained in I^{n+1}Mt^{n+1}.

Step 1.3 uses the Hilbert basis theorem (“a polynomial ring over a Noetherian ring is Noetherian”) without a cited fact. [L3] only says ideals of R are finitely generated and does not establish that polynomial rings over R are Noetherian.

[L2] omits the Axiom of Choice hypothesis of its cited corollary. It states the local-idempotent result unconditionally, while the cited item explicitly assumes AC; neither the statement nor assumptions adds AC.

Step 1.1 is invalid: the unique map \(0\to N\) is always the zero map, not a nonzero map. Exactness reflection in [L1] therefore cannot yield the asserted contradiction or establish \(N\otimes_R M\ne0\) by this argument.

Step 1.2 asserts that the graded submodule \mathcal R_N of the finite \mathcal R(I)-module \mathcal R_I(M) is finite merely because \mathcal R(I) is Noetherian. No cited fact establishes the needed submodule-finiteness theorem (or first establishes that N is finite).

The cited inverse-limit definition only defines systems indexed by \(\mathbb N_{\ge1}\), but this item uses \(\varprojlim_{n\ge0}M/F^nM\) without defining or reindexing that quotient system. Thus \(\kappa_M\)'s codomain is not supplied by its dependencies.

Step 2.1 applies [L2] to K but only asserts, without a cited fact, that the submodule K of the finite module M is finite over the Noetherian ring R. The required Noetherian submodule-finiteness result is not among the stated facts.
[L2] omits the Axiom of Choice hypothesis of its cited theorem. That theorem states the nonzero-module detection equivalence only under AC, but neither this corollary nor [L2] assumes AC.

The definition writes \(\varprojlim_{n\ge0}M/I^nM\), but its displayed quotient tower starts at \(M/IM\), and the cited inverse-system definition only covers indices \(\ge1\). No reindexing or \(M/I^0M\) stage is supplied.

[L3] misstates its citation: def-projective-object defines the lifting property, not that projectives are “allowable terms” in resolutions. This interpretive filler neither faithfully restates nor licenses the cited fact.

The definition does not establish that M/I^{n+1}M and I^nM/I^{n+1}M have finite length, so the displayed lengths are not justified. Its asserted identity also needs additivity of length along the I-adic filtration, but no such fact is cited.

[L1] is false and misstates its citation: exactness requires the image of the incoming map to equal the kernel of the outgoing map, not its cokernel to “match” that kernel. Thus step 2.1 cites an incorrect exactness criterion.
[L1] omits the Axiom of Choice hypothesis of its cited theorem. The cited detection theorem is stated under AC, but this corollary and its assumptions invoke [L1] without assuming AC.

The title says “projective covers,” but the statement and proof assume only epimorphisms from projective objects. No cover/minimality condition is stated or established, so the title asserts a stronger, different hypothesis.

Step 1.2 chooses finite generators x_1,\ldots,x_r of I, but neither [L1] nor any cited fact establishes that ideals of the given Noetherian ring R are finitely generated. This is needed to construct the finite-variable A[T]-module used in step 2.1.

[L2] inaccurately restates its Nakayama citation: the cited result assumes AC and that the module is finitely generated (as well as an ideal in the Jacobson radical). [L2] states the lifting claim without those hypotheses.

Its definition of “ideal of definition” allows I=R. For R=k, M=k\ne0, I=R, one has M/IM=0 of finite length but \chi_{I,M}=0 and P_{I,M}=0, whose degree is undefined. Thus the nonzero-M branch does not define e_I(M).

Step 2.2 asserts uniqueness, but [L4] only makes \(\widetilde f\) unique for the displayed compatible quotient maps. The proof never shows that an arbitrary \(R\)-linear \(h:\widehat M\to N\) with \(h\kappa_M=f\) induces those maps; no continuity/density condition is imposed.

[L2] omits the Axiom of Choice assumed by [[thm-jacobson-radical-unit-characterisation]]. Step 4.1 relies on that characterization, but this proposition neither assumes Choice nor cites a choice-free version.
Step 1.3 invokes Nakayama to conclude \(K=0\), but its tag cites only [L2], the equational criterion. No cited fact in that step states Nakayama’s lemma or otherwise licenses this inference.

[L2] drops a hypothesis of its citation: the cited theorem applies to every *locally small* Grothendieck abelian category (under AC), whereas [L2] states it for any Grothendieck category. The proof never establishes local smallness.

[L1] drops the cited theorem’s finite-dimensional hypothesis. Its source applies only to a Noetherian local ring of dimension d<\infty, while this theorem assumes arbitrary R and applies [L1] to A=R/Ann(M), whose dimension need not be finite.

Step 2.1 applies [L3] in ZF, but [L3] requires its new source to be projective. The $F_n$ are only free; [L2] makes them projective only under AC. Thus [L3] does not license the claimed ZF exact complex.

The statement assumes only a Noetherian ring, which here means left Noetherian and may be noncommutative. But \(\widehat M\) and the \(I\)-adic filtration cited in [L2] are defined only for a commutative ring, so the theorem is not well-formed as stated.

[L2] omits the cited theorem’s hypothesis that \(R\) is commutative. Here “Noetherian ring” may be noncommutative, so [L2] does not license tensor right exactness, and the cited adic-completion notation is not defined in that generality.

Step 1.2 does not follow from [L1]. Bounded-shift inclusions only bound the error quotient between filtration pieces; they do not show that its length has lower eventual polynomial degree. Neither [L1] nor [L2] supplies the required degree estimate.

[L2] drops the Axiom of Choice hypothesis from its cited theorem. The cited proper-ideal characterization of faithfully flat maps is explicitly stated under AC, but this example and [L2] invoke it without that assumption.
